title: Clearview AI Is Testing an AI Tool That Would Let Cops Unearth Your Life Online
gist: Clearview AI has built and tested an unreleased AI agent called InquiryIQ that takes a face-recognition hit and autonomously fans out across the web to assemble a subject profile of employers, aliases, associates and addresses, with a model selector listing xAI and Amazon Bedrock. The company's database has grown from 3 billion scraped images in 2020 to over 70 billion across more than 2,000 police agencies, and legal scholars argue the labor friction that historically served as the real privacy protection is exactly what the tool eliminates.

insights.claim: Clearview AI has built and tested an experimental AI analyst assistant, called InquiryIQ, designed to take details from a face-recognition search and automatically fan out across the web — opening pages, analyzing images, and assembling a profile of possible employers, aliases, associates and physical characteristics.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: The surveillance stack is moving from identification to autonomous dossier assembly, expanding the addressable product from a lookup tool to an analyst-replacement subscription.
insights.quote: automatically discover and enrich personal data from web sources.
insights.locator: In 2020, face-recognition firm Clearview AI became infamous

insights.claim: The tool is designed to build what the company calls a Candidate Graph of possible identities and associates while populating a subject profile with possible addresses, phone numbers, employers, social media accounts, arrest history and aliases.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Graph-of-associates output is the highest-value and highest-risk surveillance artifact, because it sweeps in people who were never investigated.
insights.locator: The code WIRED reviewed describes InquiryIQ

insights.claim: The tool's interface tells investigators that supplying age, gender and race helps the system make smarter decisions when running its searches, making protected demographic characteristics an explicit input to automated lead generation.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Race as a declared model input is the single most litigable design choice here and the most likely trigger for regulatory or civil-rights action against the category.

insights.claim: The design framing is hypothesis testing: the system takes a factoid an investigator flagged, runs searches around it, and asks whether the result is related or not, in order to validate or invalidate a proposition.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Framing autonomous search as hypothesis invalidation is the compliance narrative vendors will use to distinguish their tools from dragnet surveillance.
insights.locator: Signals and Noise

insights.claim: Clearview says InquiryIQ is a prototype that has never been pitched or shipped to customers, is not currently planned for release in its present form, and that no law enforcement user has ever used it.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: The denial defines the disclosure risk: if any deployment evidence later surfaces, the company faces a credibility problem on top of the underlying privacy issue.
insights.quote: No law enforcement user has ever used it, period,

insights.claim: Clearview argues that interface completeness no longer signals release readiness, because modern AI tools make sophisticated prototypes much faster to build and its engineers are directed to move prototypes along rapidly for that reason.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Collapsed prototyping cost changes competitive dynamics across software: finished-looking products no longer indicate commitment, roadmap or engineering investment.

themes.theme: Friction removal as the core privacy risk

insights.claim: Compressing days or weeks of detective work into minutes does not only speed up legitimate investigations — it lowers the cost of fishing expeditions, making it practical to scrutinize people police would otherwise never have investigated.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Cost-per-investigation collapsing is the mechanism that expands surveillance volume; total surveilled population scales inversely with that cost.
insights.locator: Experts say InquiryIQ and tools like it could reshape police investigations

insights.claim: Existing privacy protections were built for a world that assumed a certain amount of friction in government data collection, so many rules were never written because practical barriers made them unnecessary.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: The legal vacuum is structural, not accidental — meaning new legislation, not enforcement of existing law, is the binding constraint on this market.
insights.quote: The privacy protections we have in place right now were mainly built in a world that assumed a certain amount of friction in the ability of governments to collect information about people,
insights.locator: Woodrow Hartzog, a Boston University privacy scholar

insights.claim: The practice of assembling a person's profile from scattered digital clues left across the internet is characterized as digital rummaging, gathering information that once lived in separate places and was difficult to connect.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A named legal framing is how a practice becomes litigable; watch for digital rummaging appearing in Fourth Amendment briefing.
insights.quote: They're basically going to create a profile of you based on all of the random digital clues you left on the internet,
insights.locator: Andrew Guthrie Ferguson, a George Washington University law professor

insights.claim: Because generative AI can produce different answers from the same starting point, it may be difficult to reconstruct after the fact why an investigative system pursued one lead instead of another.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Non-determinism breaks the reconstructability that due process assumes, creating an evidentiary challenge every defense bar will eventually raise.
insights.locator: Experts say InquiryIQ and tools like it could reshape police investigations

insights.claim: The system requires an officer to accept or reject each surfaced finding and to attest they independently verified it, and the company warns that automatically generated demographic, social media and arrest data may or may not be accurate.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Attestation-based controls shift liability to the individual officer, which is exactly what makes them attractive to vendors and weak as a safeguard.

insights.claim: Over time investigators defer to automated systems until the person checking the machine becomes a rubber stamp, making human review cold comfort as a safeguard.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Automation bias undermines the single control that every AI-in-high-stakes product relies on for its regulatory defense.

insights.claim: In a Minnesota case involving undercover Homeland Security Investigations agents surveilling political activists, a Clearview report drew matches from roughly 15 years of protest photography and every result was stamped as accepted by a single named user, including one the company itself labeled a less likely result — which can only be exported if a user accepts it.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A documented instance of blanket acceptance is empirical proof that the human-review control already fails in practice, not just in theory.

insights.so_what: A greater than 20x data expansion despite lawsuits and regulatory investigations shows enforcement action failed to constrain the underlying asset accumulation.

insights.so_what: Deploy-then-govern is the historical base rate, implying revenue arrives well before regulatory cost — but also that the eventual regulatory cost is back-loaded, not avoided.
